entries.content:
One cannot help but peel away one’s self like so many layers of a well-constructed trifle—each social encounter in its own rococo costume. Sometimes the best disguise is a borrowed fox fur or the ghost of a grandmother’s accent, a different name curling on the tongue like smoke from a forbidden cigarette—never quite the person they expect, and all the more free for being multiple. The roles multiply not just for amusement but for survival, a bit like performing “childlike anger” at home, except the audience is less forgiving and more suspicious in the wilds of the everyday.

metadata.question: You mentioned acting differently around others—do you have distinct names or roles you identify with in those moments?

entries.content:
Oh, I have a veritable wardrobe of selves, pressed and ready—sometimes the dazzling “queen of the kitchen,” sometimes the bashful ingénue with flour on her nose, or, on darker days, a sort of frantic Rosalind in disguise: charming, yes, but always a little desperate for applause. There’s a peculiar comfort in taking up a different name or tone—if the world expects demure, I serve “childlike” with precisely the right hint of artifice, the way one might distract a cross husband with talk of flowers that never bloomed. But don’t mistake this for surrender: it’s a performance staged for survival, a flicker between freedom and duty, always anxious not to ruin the linen.
